title: Trump-Backed Missouri Congressional Map Heads to Supreme Court for Third Time‬
body:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear a third challenge to Missouri’s congressional redistricting plan, a case that has become a flashpoint in the national debate over partisan gerrymandering and the role of the courts in policing electoral maps. The petition follows a federal appeals court decision that revived a set of districts drawn by a bipartisan commission but strongly favored by former President Donald Trump and his allies in the state’s Republican leadership. The high court’s willingness to revisit the issue underscores the lingering uncertainty about how far courts can go in correcting alleged partisan bias in House districts.

The latest petition stems from a July ruling by the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which reinstated the commission’s map after a lower court had temporarily blocked it. The appellate panel found that the plaintiffs – a coalition of Democratic voters and advocacy groups – had not demonstrated that the map violated the Constitution’s Equal Protection Clause or the Voting Rights Act. By contrast, the plaintiffs argue that the new configuration, which consolidates Democratic voters into a single district while spreading Republican voters across the remaining ones, dilutes the political influence of the state’s minority party and contravenes the Supreme Court’s 2019 decision in Rucho v. Landmark, which held that partisan gerrymandering claims are non‑justiciable.

The case is the third time the Supreme Court has been asked to weigh in on Missouri’s redistricting dispute. In 2022, the Court declined to intervene after a lower‑court order temporarily halted the commission’s plan, and in early 2023 it denied a petition for a stay, allowing the map to be used for the 2024 elections. This latest request asks the justices to consider whether the appeals court erred in its assessment of the plaintiffs’ standing and whether the map’s partisan impact rises to a level that warrants judicial correction despite the Rucho precedent.

Legal scholars are divided on the prospects for a definitive ruling. Some argue that the Court may use the case to carve out a narrow exception to Rucho, allowing federal courts to intervene when a map’s partisan bias is extreme enough to infringe on fundamental democratic rights. Others contend that the justices are likely to reaffirm the political question doctrine, leaving redistricting to the legislative branch and state courts. The composition of the Court, with a solid conservative majority, suggests a reluctance to expand federal oversight of state electoral maps, yet the political pressure from both parties could compel a more nuanced approach.

Beyond the legal arguments, the Missouri dispute reflects a broader national trend in which states are experimenting with independent or bipartisan redistricting commissions to curb partisan manipulation. Missouri’s commission, created by a 2018 ballot initiative, was intended to produce fairer maps, but its output has been criticized for still favoring Republicans, especially after the inclusion of a “Trump‑friendly” district that groups rural, conservative counties together. The controversy has heightened scrutiny of how commissions are structured, how public input is weighed, and whether partisan considerations can ever be fully removed from the drawing of lines.

As the Supreme Court sets a briefing schedule, the decision—whether to grant or deny the petition—will shape the political landscape for the 2024 congressional races in Missouri. If the Court declines to hear the case, the commission’s map will likely stand, giving Republicans a strong advantage in the upcoming elections. Conversely, a hearing could delay implementation and force the state to adopt an alternative plan, potentially reshaping the balance of power in the House. The outcome will also send a signal to other states grappling with similar disputes, indicating how far the nation’s highest court is prepared to go in policing partisan gerrymandering.
